title: The Gender Trap: Why We Are Seduced by Obvious Explanations
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau examines the cognitive trap schools fall into when analyzing gender gaps in exam results: jumping from a visible pattern (boys underperform girls) directly to gender-based explanations, bypassing competing variables such as attendance, prior attainment, reading age, class allocation, teacher absence, curriculum time, and option choices. Drawing on Belgian psychologist Albert Michotte's work on the perception of causality, Didau shows that human brains are wired to perceive causal relationships in sequential events even when none exist—turning observational patterns into confident explanations before evidence warrants it. He then introduces Hume's is-ought gap: observing that boys underperform does not, without a separate moral judgment, tell us what schools should do. Schools repeatedly commit two fallacies—the naturalistic fallacy (boys are more restless, therefore schools should be redesigned around restlessness) and the moralistic fallacy (children ought to be capable of X, therefore they are). The existence of a tendency provides constraints but not policies; evidence-based improvement requires actively questioning whether a pattern is even meaningful once other variables are controlled.
points: * Schools systematically bypass competing variables (attendance, prior attainment, reading age, teacher absence, curriculum time) when explaining gender gaps, defaulting to the most psychologically available cause. * Albert Michotte's 1940s experiments demonstrated that humans perceive causality in sequential events even without logical grounds—the same illusion operates when teachers and leaders read classroom patterns. * Hume's is-ought gap: describing a pattern (boys underperform) does not, without a separate moral claim, tell us what should be done—a value judgment must be explicitly added and defended. * The naturalistic fallacy (boys are restless, so schools should accommodate restlessness) and the moralistic fallacy (children should succeed, so academic expectations must be lowered) both appear regularly in educational gender discourse. * Evidence-based school improvement requires actively resisting the most convenient explanation and interrogating whether a gap is meaningful once other variables are controlled—not treating every visible pattern as a mandate for policy.
quotes: Before we've considered attendance, prior attainment, reading age, class allocation, teacher absence, behaviour, curriculum time, option choices, or whether the difference is meaningful once other variables are considered, we default to the most obvious cause: there's something about gender that causes boys to do less well than girls in school.
Causality cannot be directly observed, only inferred. Yet some sequences are so compelling that our inferences feel like perception.

In A Treatise of Human Nature, published in 1739-40, David Hume noticed that writers often begin by describing how the world is, then suddenly start telling us how it ought to be, without explaining the move.
A pattern exists, therefore it must be accepted, accommodated and declared inevitable. But the existence of a tendency doesn't tell us how to respond to it.

We begin with something visible: a gap, a pattern, a graph, a behaviour, a lesson that went badly and then we add in the most convenient, plausible explanation because it fits what we already believe. Once an explanation feels plausible, it becomes true.
